items.article_search_text: The McLaren CEO assures that the Australian is recovering his confidence and performance after a complicated start to the season. Zak Brown has launched a message of optimism about Oscar Piastri's future at McLaren [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/mclaren]. The British team's CEO considers that the Australian driver is recovering the confidence and performance that made him one of the most promising drivers on the grid, after an especially complicated start to the 2026 season: "I think so; he is becoming the driver I know again. With these cars, the field has gotten a bit mixed up, right? Lewis Hamilton is getting more out of the Ferrari now. George Russell got more out of the car last year than Kimi Antonelli; that has changed. I think these cars are so complex that some drivers have adapted a little faster than others, but I like what I'm seeing from Oscar; he feels more confident and in control. I like where our two drivers are now," Brown declared at the Friday press conference in Singapore. Piastri's season has been marked by his struggle to adapt to the new generation of cars. After finishing third in the drivers' championship in 2025, the Australian has struggled to extract consistent performance from the MCL40. Although he has achieved two podiums this year, he has not matched the pace of his teammate, Lando Norris, who has added two Grand Prix victories and has beaten him in qualifying in 11 of the 17 rounds contested so far. Stella and Norris’s Maturity: 'He Set Aside His Interests' [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/fc709052-dc86-4aeb-b701-0a7c81d49ea2.jpeg] Stella and Norris’s Maturity: 'He Set Aside His Interests' The McLaren director praises the champion for helping Piastri finish fifth in Singapore after the crash that took them out of the fight. [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/stella-and-norris-s-maturity-he-set-aside-his-interests] Andrea Stella [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/stella-and-norris-s-maturity-he-set-aside-his-interests], McLaren team boss, had already explained that Piastri was having difficulties driving by "pure instinct" in certain conditions, a situation that the driver himself acknowledged before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix: "Many of the things that had worked for me previously don't seem to work this year, so it's about trying to find others that do. I'm making progress on that, but it is not as simple as finding a direction that works for you all the time. You need to adapt and change things constantly," Piastri explained. Despite the ups and downs, the Australian has shown signs of recovery in the last races, at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia he finished sixth after a complicated afternoon in Sepang where a decision to start on medium tires in wet conditions forced him to enter the pits earlier than planned, however he showed himself satisfied with his own performance, later at the Singapore Grand Prix, he finished fifth after an eventful race, in which he retired from the Sprint due to a crash with Norris on the last lap and suffered a slow puncture on Sunday that forced him to make an unscheduled stop, despite everything, he managed to overtake Hamilton on the last lap to take fifth position. Ranking the Best 25-and-Under Current F1 Drivers [https://deweb-519a7.b-cdn.net/post-images/1df5bb79-8505-4430-a7df-372c770a407f.jpeg] Ranking the Best 25-and-Under Current F1 Drivers Two obvious names are at the top of the best 25-and-under Formula 1 drivers. But how does the rest of the list shape up? [https://roundtable.io/sports/f1/news/ranking-the-best-25-and-under-current-f1-drivers] "It was quite reasonable, I would say; I think we simply didn't have enough pace. We couldn't follow Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc; I think Kimi was also a little faster than us. There wasn't much we could do beyond where we finished," Piastri reflected. Brown, for his part, trusts that McLaren can maintain its progress in the final stretch of the season: "The objective is to arrive at every weekend with the possibility of winning; we feel more in control of things than in the last races, and we won the two before those. It shows how competitive the sport is and how fast the top four teams, and the whole grid, move up and down the competitiveness ladder. Our objective is to try to arrive at every race weekend and win, but that is easier said than done," Brown concluded.

McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella has identified what he believes is the root of Oscar Piastri 's ongoing struggles to find success in the 2026 season . Stella said that he believes Piastri's 'signature' clean driving style has not matched the MCL40 as well as its predecessor. The Australian earned seven Grand Prix victories in 2025, leading the Driver's Championship for much of the season before losing out to teammate Lando Norris. However so far in 2026, Piastri has only two podiums to his name, with the most recent being in Miami back in May. Stella thinks that Piastri is simply taking longer to adapt his driving style to the new era of cars, as he explained to the media in Singapore. "The car needs quite a lot of effort to deliver lap time, and it requires a level of intensity in the driving input, which is much superior to last year," he said. "This is something that took some time for the drivers to get comfortable. Well, comfortable is wrong, but to get to understand, and it's also one of the reasons why Oscar almost looks like he lost some of the competitiveness compared to Lando. "We were discussing what is happening with Oscar, and I've always said that that was a technical matter. Oscar just needed to understand how to force the car to do some things and sort of abandon the fact that driving fast will not necessarily mean driving clean. "Instead, probably the signature of Oscar, when we have seen him fast in the past, was that he was clean. It was really good data to see. "It was very repeatable, and it was fast. With this car, all these things together don't seem to happen very often. So it's a lot of work for the drivers." Oscar Piastri has only managed two podiums so far this season Stella not expecting upgrades miracles for either Oscar Piastri or Lando Norris McLaren has confirmed that it will bring a new upgrade package at some point before the end of the season, but Stella does not believe this will make it easier to drive. "I don't expect that what's coming to the car will improve this characteristic. "I think we need something more fundamental than simply adding some downforce to the car, like it's happening in the coming races, without fundamentally changing some further aspect, which we are addressing longer term, I would say with the MCL41 for 2027." items.article_search_text: Lando Norris apologized after colliding with Oscar Piastri in Singapore, while Andrea Stella reaffirmed McLaren's commitment to equal treatment and team unity. McLaren has reaffirmed its commitment to equal treatment for Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri after their collision in the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race exposed tensions between individual ambition and team priorities. The incident on the final lap cost the team valuable points, prompting team principal Andrea Stella to demand greater unity from both drivers before the main race.Norris attempted to overtake Piastri at Turn Five, but the two McLaren cars made contact and spun. Piastri hit the barriers and retired, while Norris recovered to finish eighth, scoring one point. According to BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson, the team lost the opportunity to collect nine points from the sprint.Norris initially defended his decision to attempt the pass, arguing that the move was permitted under racing guidelines. However, he later accepted responsibility, acknowledging that his personal ambitions should not have taken priority over McLaren's collective interests.After the race, Norris admitted the attempt was unnecessary and apologized to the team. He also offered to help Piastri during the Grand Prix when the Australian was trying to recover from a slow puncture and an additional pit stop.Speaking after the Grand Prix, Norris explained that Piastri had been unfortunate with the puncture and that his own car had experienced problems. With several cars separating them and little realistic opportunity for Norris to catch Kimi Antonelli, he believed helping his teammate offered a better chance of maximizing McLaren's points.Stella welcomed the change in approach, saying the team had already discussed the sprint collision with both drivers. He emphasized that the central issue was not whether Norris had been alongside Piastri during the attempted pass, but whether both drivers consistently prioritized the team over individual interests.The McLaren team principal maintained that the organization would continue treating its drivers fairly and would not abandon its policy of equal status. He also said further discussions were necessary to strengthen cooperation between the drivers and the wider team.Former Haas team principal Guenther Steiner criticized Norris's decision during an appearance on The Red Flags Podcast, describing the incident as a mistake inconsistent with the judgment expected from a world champion. Steiner also praised Stella's handling of the situation, arguing that Norris ultimately recognized the unnecessary risk and the importance of his subsequent response.Despite the sprint collision, McLaren recovered in Sunday's Grand Prix, with Norris finishing fourth and Piastri fifth. According to Formula1.com, the result restored the positions the pair had effectively lost through the previous day's incident and gave the team a stronger points return.Stella said McLaren's strategy had been designed to maximize the drivers' opportunities at the start. Both cars began on soft tires because the team believed the medium compound could leave them vulnerable to losing positions and being forced into an early pit stop.McLaren subsequently extended its opening stint in the hope that a Safety Car would reduce the time lost during a pit stop. No Safety Car appeared, and the team ultimately finished behind Red Bull, Ferrari and Mercedes, according to Formula1.com.Stella considered fourth and fifth the best realistic result on performance, although he acknowledged that Norris might have had an opportunity to challenge Antonelli for a podium position under different circumstances. He also pointed to planned car upgrades as a potential improvement for the team's upcoming races.Motorsport.com reported that Norris and Piastri collected 22 points combined in the Grand Prix after scoring only one point in the sprint. The result gave McLaren an opportunity to move forward after a difficult weekend while the team continued addressing the lessons from the collision.

Running fourth and fifth in the 20-lap prelude to Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix , Norris began swarming all over the back of his team. This culminated in a risky move on a partly damp track with Norris sticking his MCL40 up the inside of the Australian at Turn 5. Piastri's sister car was prodded sideways, with both spinning and eventually facing backwards, and almost collected by the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson. Norris got going again and finished eighth for one point, whereas Piastri retired on the spot. "I’m going to imagine [there were] some fairly stern words last night to your drivers, who managed to trip over each other," Brundle commented. "Oh yeah," Brown admitted. "That was a ‘don’t do that again.’ And we didn’t say 'please'. 'That’s an order'." The move cost McLaren eight World Championship points, as the race for 'best of the rest' in the Constructors' Championship hots up between the Woking-based squad, Ferrari and Red Bull. "Yeah. Two years after their karting showdown, the Quad Lock athletes have traded Grand Prix machinery for identical off-road buggies in Young Guns Part 2. Three challenges, one motocro Young Guns Part 2: Oscar Piastri vs Pedro Acosta, the Off-Road Rematch Formula 1 driver Oscar Piastri and MotoGP rider Pedro Acosta are back. Two years after their karting showdown, the Quad Lock athletes have traded Grand Prix machinery for identical off-road buggies in Young Guns Part 2. Three challenges, one motocross track, and one winner. Where it started: Young Guns Part 1 In 2024, Quad Lock brought Piastri and Acosta together for the first Young Guns film. It was a karting challenge in France, with Acosta driving a kart for the first time. Piastri came out on top. A lot has happened since. Piastri is now a nine-time Formula 1 Grand Prix winner with the McLaren Mastercard Formula 1 Team. Acosta won his first MotoGP Grand Prix in Austria in September 2026 and is one of the championship’s standout young talents. F1 vs MotoGP on dirt For Part 2, the pair left the tarmac behind. Young Guns Part 2 was filmed on 14 August 2026 at Monti MX, a motocross circuit in the hills above Menton on the French Riviera. The track is hard-packed, rutted and full of jumps. Piastri and Acosta raced matching Segway Super Villain buggies, which took both of them out of their usual disciplines. Four wheels suit Piastri, and dirt suits Acosta. Neither of them races buggies. “Last time it was karting, which is pretty much home turf for me, so I had a bit of an advantage,” said Piastri. “This time Pedro probably had the edge, with the dirt and the jumps. I’ll let people watch and decide who handled it better.” “I always have a good time with Oscar,” said Acosta. “We laughed a lot making the first video, and this one was the same. Being on the dirt with the buggies was something different for us, and the track at Monti is amazing.” Hosted by Charley Boorman Long-time Quad Lock ambassador, adventure rider and TV presenter Charley Boorman hosts the showdown. He takes the pair through each challenge and catches the moments between runs. The film combines on-board cameras, drones and trackside footage with candid moments away from a Grand Prix weekend. It is Quad Lock’s most ambitious production to date. Quad Lock mounts, put to the test The phones in Young Guns Part 2 weren’t props. Both buggies ran Quad Lock mounts, and the phones were part of the challenges themselves, so they had to take the vibration, impacts and jumps of a full motocross circuit. “Our product is integrated into the challenges because that is where it belongs,” said Dom Storey, Global Head of Sports Marketing at Quad Lock. Norris and Piastri made contact on the last lap of Saturday's shortened race when battling for fourth, which the stewards did not penalise either driver for. However, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella labelled the incident as "not acceptable" while Norris was not keen to talk about the collision on Saturday and told Sky Sports F1 : "As a team we all spoke about it. I apologised but that's all you need to know." "It's pretty straightforward. I can't attempt what I did. I should never have attempted in the first place, even if the move was on. I've got to think of the team that I represent more than myself," he said. "It was a mistake on my part, and I let down the team. I've also apologised to all of them, I owe them all an apology, and I will do better next time." Stella: Conversations with drivers not finished During Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix, Norris asked several times if he could aid team-mate Piastri in any way during the closing stages of the race. Piastri was attempting to catch and overtake Lewis Hamilton at the time of the radio calls, suggesting Norris was querying whether he should back up the Ferrari driver. In the end, Piastri overtook Hamilton without any help to finish fifth behind Norris. Stella says he was "very encouraged" by Norris' willingness to aid his team-mate but more talks will be held before the United States Grand Prix in Austin next weekend. "We are aligned as to how we want to lead this team forward in a joint effort between the team and the drivers," he said. "The conversations that we are having, they are not finished but it's not because we need to go back discussing if Lando was alongside Oscar, that's not the interesting bit. "For me the interesting bit is a reflection that all the stakeholders, the team, the drivers will have to make around leading together the team, embracing constantly from inside the cockpit the interest of the team, as something that is superior to any particular singular individual interest. "While the conversations from this point of view, they are not concluded and there's more we can do to become a more united and even stronger team, I'm pleased that Lando at some stage in the race adopted this way of thinking. "This is what I expect as a team principal, this is what the 1000 people that work at McLaren expect from our drivers so it's good that we read this example. I expect definitely more of that in the future, independently of the fact that they will be heard in the radio, or they will happen behind the closed door in every meeting or in the way we approach our race plan." items.article_search_text: Sky Sports F1s Martin Brundle gives his verdict on Max Verstappens dominant weekend in Singapore, Lewis Hamiltons decision to not pit under a Virtual Safety Car and the Sprint collision between McLarens Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri It was a full-on weekend of F1, with a Sprint race added to the street circuit schedule. Coming at the end of a demanding run of six Grands Prix in seven weeks, it was a significant challenge for everyone involved, not just the teams and drivers. I've always enjoyed the Singapore Grand Prix, right from the first race, despite the relentless heat and humidity that can leave you feeling like you need a shower barely five minutes into the day. The city is buzzing, the event has a fantastic atmosphere and the F1 cars are relentlessly pounding around the circuit. With just one practice session followed by two qualifying sessions and two races, it makes for an action-packed weekend. However, what took the shine off things a little this year was the unusually poor air quality caused by crop burning in neighbouring countries. Singapore has long held the mantle as F1's 'business' Grand Prix, combining world-class motorsport with a top-tier music festival. A record combined crowd of more than 300,000 underlined its appeal, making it an event well worth adding to your bucket list if you haven't already been. Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 Russell's Sprint crash sums up his season It was very much Max Verstappen and Red Bull's weekend, with the Dutchman winning both the Sprint and the Grand Prix from pole position. Combined with his victory at Sepang in Malaysia a few days earlier, that made it three wins in a row. Verstappen is still too far behind to mount another 'Chucky' championship comeback like last season, but he has climbed to fourth in the standings, just eight points behind Lewis Hamilton and 17 behind second-placed George Russell. However, he remains 119 points adrift of championship leader Kimi Antonelli, with 150 points still available, assuming all the remaining races go ahead amid ongoing global conflicts. After a surprise storm delay and a couple of laps behind the Safety Car, the Sprint finally got under way. George made an impressive start to take the lead from second on the grid, but carried too much speed and throttle into the pit straight at the end of the opening lap, spinning into the concrete barriers. With major power unit penalties already looming for the Grand Prix, this was his best opportunity to make an impact. The images of him sliding across the white line and wet kerbs felt like a fitting summary of his season so far. This left Max out in front, with Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari keeping him honest, while Charles Leclerc began to drop back in the second Ferrari as he struggled more than most with his worn intermediate tyres. Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris kept a close watch in their McLarens, which had shown strong pace throughout the weekend. Both were closing in on Leclerc, with Antonelli's Mercedes also being drawn into the battle. However, with the track still damp and the kerbs slippery, there was little incentive to take unnecessary risks with the main qualifying session and Grand Prix still to come. The priority was to bring the cars home safely and collect whatever Sprint points were on offer, before attention turned to the bigger prizes ahead. Norris' overtake attempt on Piastri a lunge too far Lando had other ideas. He had looked a little quicker than Oscar throughout, although not quite enough to overtake easily. Heading into Turn 5 on the final lap, having seemingly been sizing up the move for several laps, Norris sliced down Oscar's right-hand side to claim the corner and position. The pair touched and spun in a synchronised pirouette, with Piastri's car hitting the wall. McLaren are in a battle now with Red Bull for third in the championship when not so long ago they were catching Ferrari in a battle for second. These positions mean huge amounts prize money for 2027, along with the kudos and season long pitlane position, and likely partner/sponsor bonuses. Money and resource spent on 2026 parts can also impact on the 2027 car now. The team didn't care which driver was in front, they just wanted them home undamaged in fourth and fifth. The only consolation was Lando recovered for a point in eighth. Drivers are hard wired to simply race, and think of their own goals, that's why they do what they do, but whilst there was a gap against his team-mate, who could perhaps have given more space assuming he even saw it coming, it was a risky move and a lunge too far from Lando. We understand McLaren team bosses were extremely unhappy with that one. Through all the chaos Antonelli steered nicely around everything to claim a fortunate third from seventh on the Sprint grid yet again extending his championship lead. His patience continues to pay off. Verstappen had all bases covered Having never taken pole position in Singapore before, Max Verstappen followed up his Sprint success by securing pole for the main race. The data suggested that either Ferrari could have claimed pole had they extracted the full potential from their laps. Regardless, Charles Leclerc came close to beating Verstappen to the first corner, but the Red Bull driver had the advantage of a fresh set of soft tyres and used them to squeeze Leclerc into submission. The field settled into race order relatively quickly. Starting from the back, George Russell could only climb to 17th in the opening stages, such was the intensity and competitiveness of the midfield. Isack Hadjar, starting from the pitlane in the similarly displaced Red Bull, faced an even tougher challenge. This is a good opportunity to give Liam Lawson a deserved shout-out. Driving for Racing Bulls, he finished seventh in the challenging conditions at Sepang the previous week, followed that up with fifth in the Singapore Sprint and then secured another seventh-place finish in Sunday's Grand Prix. As the highest-placed driver outside the top four teams, Lawson put together an excellent run across a demanding series of races. Out front, Verstappen had the Grand Prix firmly under control. Although Leclerc kept him honest in the opening stages, the Dutchman was eventually able to build a comfortable gap, giving Red Bull greater flexibility with its strategy and the freedom to react calmly to the tactics of its rivals or the potential intervention of a Safety Car. Impossible to run a modern F1 car and team from behind the wheel Hamilton started on a fresh set of medium tyres but began to struggle as the race progressed. Appearing to be on a clear two-stop strategy, he pitted as early as lap 18 for soft tyres. Bizarrely, he would not stop again, despite the opportunity to make a relatively cheap pit stop under a Virtual Safety Car (VSC) when Lance Stroll's stricken Aston Martin had to be cleared from the circuit. Hamilton then endured a relentless slide down the order, eventually losing fifth place to Oscar Piastri's McLaren in the closing stages, despite the Australian having made an unscheduled stop for a slow puncture. After the race, it emerged that switching to a one-stop strategy, which required him to complete 44 laps on the same tyres, had been Hamilton's own decision. He apologised to the team for the call. It is difficult to run a modern F1 car and manage the team's strategy from behind the wheel, and the incident was telling. Ferrari had seemingly expected Hamilton to pit under the VSC. Lando Norris had been pressuring the struggling Hamilton before making a late move down the inside into Turn 1. Both drivers ran wide, Hamilton more so, and as they scrambled back onto the circuit with dirty tyres, championship leader Kimi Antonelli seized his opportunity to sweep past them both. The move secured him third place, ahead of his two closest title rivals, and extended his championship lead once again. It was an impressive display of maturity, particularly given that Mercedes no longer appears to have the fastest car on the grid. Norris and Piastri secured a solid fourth and fifth for McLaren, while a tenacious drive from Nico Hulkenberg in his Audi limited George Russell to just two points in ninth. Isack Hadjar claimed the final point in 10th after starting from the pitlane in his Red Bull, capping an impressive recovery drive. Oscar Piastri has battled to a hard-fought fifth place at the Singapore Grand Prix, helping his McLaren team salvage some pride and useful championship points from an otherwise frustrating weekend at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Australian star Piastri finished one place behind team-mate Lando Norris, just outside the podium spots, but the day after both McLaren drivers received a public dressing down from team chiefs for a collision between them on the final lap of Saturday’s Sprint race, the Grand Prix result can be judged a positive outcome. The weekend, however, really belonged to Red Bull flyer Max Verstappen, who roared home to victory on his 250th Grand Prix start, capping a remarkable 24 hours in which the four-time world champ also banked two pole positions and a classy victory in the Sprint race. Starting from his 50th career pole place, it was the Dutchman’s second straight victory after winning the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend, and leaves him fourth in the championship standings. Verstappen’s triumph means Red Bull are now seven points behind constructors’ champions McLaren in the battle for third place. “It’s taken a while but I think this race was very good. We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre, even though I think the medium tyre for everyone was more of a struggle,” Verstappen said. “But it worked out, so of course very happy to win here... The last two races have been really positive for us and it’s just great to see.” Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc finished second while Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli was third, extending his championship lead over teammate George Russell to 102 points and knowing he can mathematically win his maiden title in the next round in Austin, Texas from 23-25 October. “Can I? Really?”, 20-year-old Italian Antonelli said when he was told after his 14th podium of the season. “Well, let’s not worry about that. Let’s try to do the best weekend as possible and finish the job.” Meanwhile, once Norris knew he had lost out to Antonelli when battling Lewis Hamilton for the final podium slot, McLaren’s reigning world champion offered to ease up and help teammate Piastri as the race reached its climax. But 25-year-old Melburnian Piastri, despite suffering bad luck when forced to pit a second time thanks to a slow puncture, still had the composure to do it his own way, overtaking seven-time champion Hamilton on the final lap. “The puncture was a shame, but I think fifth place was the maximum we could have done today,” Piastri said. “We didn’t quite have the pace to challenge the Red Bull and the Ferraris, although being able to get that final position from Lewis made it worthwhile. It was a reasonable chunk of points for the team.” Veteran Briton Hamilton endured a frustrating end to the race in his Ferrari, the 41-year-old struggling with worn tyres as Norris also went past him. Hamilton, who missed his post-race media duties after feeling unwell, earlier admitted it had been his choice to stay on older tyres rather than risk losing position with a second pit stop. “Sorry boys, I let you down today with that strategy. My call and I lost us valuable points,” Hamilton said. “I’ll try and make up for it in the next one.” Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur stressed that there was no blame on the team. “We asked him (Hamilton) to pit. Don’t blame the team guys, clearly on the radio he apologised and said ‘it was my call’,” Vasseur said. "We didn't quite have the pace to challenge the Red Bull and the Ferraris, although being able to get that final position from Lewis made it worthwhile. It was a reasonable chunk of points for the team." Veteran Briton Hamilton endured a frustrating end to the race in his Ferrari, the 41-year-old struggling with worn tyres as Norris also went past him. Hamilton, who missed his post-race media duties after feeling unwell, earlier admitted it had been his choice to stay on older tyres rather than risk losing position with a second pit stop. "Sorry boys, I let you down today with that strategy. My call and I lost us valuable points," Hamilton said. "I'll try and make up for it in the next one." The Australian was keen to recover from the misery of being punted out of Saturday's Sprint Race by teammate Lando Norris, costing the Woking-based squad eight points. On race day, the MCL40 was once again a tricky car to negotiate around the Marina Bay Circuit, but Norris and Piastri avoided trouble to take a double-points finish. Piastri suffered a slow puncture earlier in the race, which forced an unplanned tyre stop, and after that, suffered a slow release of his front-right in the next stop. But shrugging off these obstacles, Piastri bore down on Lewis Hamilton in the closing laps, the Brit having opted to stay out during a VSC, which left him vulnerable as his rubber degraded. Piastri duly overtook the Ferrari driver to finish P5, and speaking after the race, took pride from his own personal performance. "I feel like personally, I did a really good job," he said. "Obviously, the puncture was a bit of a shame, but ironically I think it actually helped me get Lewis at the end, so it was a silver lining." After the collision yesterday between himself and teammate Lando Norris, the McLaren driver concluded that it left them at a pace disadvantage. Oscar Piastri made the best of bad circumstances to finish in P5 "It was definitely the most we could have done," the #81 driver said. "We didn't have the pace to do anymore and he has a massive track record in this race." Piastri added: "It was tough. "Once you get there, it doesn't take much to overheat the tyres and you kind of get stuck at their pace. But with how quickly I was catching, I would have been disappointed if I didn't get past. "A bit of excitement which was good, because otherwise it was a pretty lonely race." Another tinge of irony is that Norris and Piastri finished fourth and fifth, the positions they ought to have finished in the day before had their intra-team collision not occurred. Follow this live blog for minute-by-minute updates, scores, results, odds, starting grid, crash updates and start time A blistering Max Verstappen led every single lap from pole, triumphing in Singapore, while a luckless Oscar Piastri was plagued by a slow pitstop. Thanks so much for joining us folks. Join us on October 25 for the United States Grand Prix in Texas. With five laps to go of the Singapore Grand Prix, Lando Norris radioed his engineer asking an important question. The McLaren driver was sitting in fourth and did not have the pace to challenge championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third. “Is there anyway to help out behind or not,” he asked, referring to his teammate Oscar Piastri who was stuck in sixth behind Lewis Hamilton, who was dropping paces due to tyre degradation Norris tried again a few laps later. “Shall I try and help Oscar out or not,” Norris said over the radio. “No keep going,” his engineer replied. Norris’ repeated offers of help were the signs of a good teammate, but also could represent a sheepish driver, who as F1 commentator Martin Brundle noted was trying to “get back in McLaren’s good books”. Piastri didn’t end up needing his teammate help, overtaking Hamilton in a last-lap battle to clinch fifth – a solid result since his race was marred by a slow pitstop and tyre puncture. A flawless Max Verstappen went on to win the Singapore Grand Prix with a blistering performance that saw him lead every lap from pole. However, a lot of attention was on the McLaren duo, Piastri and Norris following their collision during the sprint race on Saturday. Norris attempted to overtake his teammate in the final lap of the sprint, but clipped the Australian’s rear tyre with his front wheel. The impact sent Piastri spinning into the wall and knocked both papaya cars out of podium contention. Norris later copped scrutiny on social media for his comments in a post-race interview when he sarcastically responded to a journalist who implied his move was “unnecessary”. “What’s the title of the race?” he asked an interviewer. “What’s after ‘sprint’?” When the interviewer replied “race”, he laughed and sarcastically said: “Wow, good job”. Before Sunday’s main race Zak Brown was uncharacteristically open about how McLaren dealt with the situation. “That was a ‘don’t do that again’, and we didn’t say please, that’s an order,” he told Sky Sports when asked if he had stern words for the duo. “You can’t have that, it was unnecessary result for the team when a lot of pressure is on.” On Sunday, it was clear Norris had listened to the reprimands, offering repeatedly to help Piastri out. There were no collisions or racing incidents between the duo during Sunday’s race. It was ultimately a slow 4.2 second pitstop that hurt Piastri’s chances of a higher finish. The Australian was also forced to come into the pits a second time after a tyre puncture. It paints a painful picture of a 2026 season that has not gone to plan for Piastri. On the other end of the scale is Kimi Antonelli – who after finishing third in Singapore– is now mathematically capable of winning the title at the next race in Texas. If so, it would make him the youngest world champion in history. When informed of this during a post-race interview, a wide-eyed Kimi Antonelli said he had no idea. “Can I really?, ” he said. “Let’s not worry about that, let’s try to do the best job possible and finish the job.” A blistering Max Verstappen led every single lap from pole, triumphing in Singapore to win the grand prix. It was slightly awkward though.... Verstappen has been plagued by radio issues so when his engineer congratulated him, we couldn’t hear Verstappen’s response. Instead, audiences just heard a bunch of garbled noises. Oh well, I’m sure the Dutchman is pleased with that result. Charles Leclerc finished in second, with Antonelli in third, Norris fourth and Piastri in fifth. “Shall I try and help Oscar out or not,” Norris said over the radio. “No keep going,” his engineer replied. After stalking the Ferrari for several laps,Piastri tried to make a move, but Hamilton had the inside line and held the spot. He goes again and HE DOES IT. The difference between Hamilton and Piastri is now less than one second. Hamilton is really paying the price for not pitting earlier. I imagine there will be heavy discussions in Ferrari strategy offices. Can Piastri snatch fifth place? That’s some good teamwork from Norris. He asks his engineer if he can do anything to help “back there” referring to Piastri trying to catch Hamilton. Might be Norris trying to get back in McLaren’s good books after that sprint race incident. Piastri is roughly five seconds behind Hamilton with three laps to go. Hamilton’s bad day is getting worse. He didn’t pit, then lost his place to his teammate. He then lost his place to Kimi Antonelli followed by Lando Norris, who waited for the perfect opportunity. The seven-time world champion is now in fifth, with Oscar Piastri behind him in sixth. Can Piastri catch Hamilton? Here comes Lando Norris. The British driver lunges towards the Ferrari, but Hamilton takes evasive action going off track to keep third place. Kimi Antonelli swoops and takes advantage and snatches fourth place off Norris. Antonelli is flying now and catches Hamilton to grab third place. Ten laps to go and Charles Leclerc has cut down Max Verstappen’s lead to roughly 9.7 seconds. Verstappen’s radio doesn’t seem to be working either, and his Red Bull engineer is trying to communicate to the driver in code. Red Bull are worried about a potential safety car, which would allow an opportunity for Leclerc to catch Verstappen. Meanwhile, Lando Norris is gaining on Hamilton. Norris has tyres that are 14 laps fresher. Unless some gigantic calamity happens.… Max Verstappen will likely win this race. Verstappen now leads Leclerc by 15 seconds, with Lewis Hamilton in third. Lando Norris is in fourth with Kimi Antonelli in fifth and Oscar Piastri in sixth. Piastri started his race in sixth so today is shaping up to be another disappointing outcome, although not of his making. He had a slow pitstop and then a tyre puncture. There’s still 12 laps to go and it’s likely Norris could catch Verstappen and snatch a podium position.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella has warned his drivers against putting personal ambitions ahead of the team after teammates Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri collided in the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race. Norris made an ambitious overtaking attempt on Piastri for fourth place on the final lap of yesterday’s sprint, but made contact with the Australian and sent both cars into a spin. Norris dropped to eighth while Piastri failed to finish, meaning McLaren collected just one point in the Formula One constructors’ standings instead of nine. After what he described as “a very long, tiring and challenging day”, Stella said he addressed the incident with both drivers. “Very simply, it is unacceptable that two McLarens ever come together on track. This is a fundamental principle of how we go racing, and something both drivers are very well aware of,” Stella said. He added: “We have reminded our drivers that the interests of the team must always come first, and that did not happen today.” Stella earlier told Sky Sports: “There’s no ego, there’s no person that’s bigger than the interest of the McLaren F1 team. This will be reiterated.” Norris told Sky’s Italian broadcast that he was “told off” over the incident. He had earlier defended the move, saying he believed it was a legitimate overtaking attempt. The stewards did not penalise Norris for causing a collision, ruling that “both drivers had contributed to the incident”. That came after Norris told the stewards he expected Piastri to leave more space, while Piastri said he was surprised by his teammate’s overtaking attempt. Qualifying brought further disappointment for McLaren, with defending champion Norris fifth and Piastri seventh. Max Verstappen won the sprint race and followed up by securing the 50th pole position of his career at the Singapore Grand Prix, a circuit where he had never previously claimed either a victory or pole. Apart from Verstappen, the day’s other big winner was Kimi Antonelli, who extended his advantage over George Russell after his Mercedes teammate crashed out from the lead in the sprint. The Italian qualified fourth, putting himself in a strong position to score valuable points in tomorrow’s race, while Russell must serve a grid penalty. An upgraded Red Bull car has played a key role in turning Verstappen’s season around, but the Dutchman says one major weakness remains. Verstappen said Red Bull will need to address its “horrendous” starts after he lost the sprint lead off the line, just as he did in Malaysia last week, where he still managed to claim his first win of the 2026 season. “We don’t accelerate off the line,” he said. “Up until now, we always have terrible starts. So we need to understand what’s going on there.”
